newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions extend Cr Foncier HQ occupation to Monday.
newsitem.headline: Unions extend Cr Foncier HQ occupation to Monday.

text.p: Trade unions and staff fighting to save troubled bank Credit Foncier de France decided on Friday to extend a week-old occupation of the Paris headquarters until Monday, a union member said.

A second negotiating session with government-appointed mediator Philippe Rouvillois was scheduled for Monday and the sit-in would go on until the government abandoned a plan to wind down part of the bank, he said.
"We'll spend the weekend at least," said the union member, speaking by telephone from the downtown Paris head office.
Unions had said on Thursday evening they believed the plan had been set aside but they appeared to change their tune with a vote on Friday morning to keep up the protest.

Several hundred staff have been occupying the headquarters of Credit Foncier since last Friday demanding that government plans unveiled by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis in July to dismantle the home loans specialist be abandoned.
"From Rouvillois's statement it is clear that the Arthuis plan is not totally cast aside," the union representative said.

Arthuis told the National Assembly on Thursday that his plan for a partial takeover by cooperatively-run property lender Credit Immobilier and a wind-down of the rest was drawn up because Foncier had no future and no one else had showed any interest in buying the bank.

The Foncier protest, in which the bank's chairman Jerome Meyssonnier was held inside the bank until Wednesday, has forced government officials right up to Prime Minister Alain Juppe to defend themselves in public and in parliament.

Juppe argued in front of the Assembly that Credit Foncier made losses of nearly 11 billion francs ($2 billion) in 1995 and would have gone bankrupt if the government had not stepped in, but that it could not expect more help from state funds.
The unions, with considerable backing from politicians on both sides of the political divide, say the 1995 accounts of Credit Foncier were overloaded to trigger its fall.
They point to predictions of a profit of one billion francs for 1996, that this is not likely to be just a one-off event, and that a far smaller amount could be needed to keep the group in business.

Credit Foncier, which was set up by emperor Napoleon III 145 years ago, has already been "nationalised" in a buyout by state bank Caisses des Depots on the government's behalf, in the first stage of the Arthuis plan.

Keeping up the heat on the government, trade unions from 14 state and semi-state banking and finance groups agreed to hold a rally on Tuesday to protest against "repeated and indescribable attacks on Credit Foncier" and job cuts across the sector.
